meta.title: Who really said "We need a revolution every 200 years"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Franklin. The phrase appears nowhere in his papers — a full-text search of Founders Online returns nothing. The genuinely adjacent line is Jefferson's, it says twenty years rather than two hundred, and it is a different quote by a different man.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We need a revolution every 200 years'?
meta.ogDescription: Franklin never wrote it — his papers are fully searchable and the phrase is not there. Jefferson said something close in 1787, but his interval was twenty years, not two hundred.

answer.label: Nobody we can name — not Franklin
answer.authorDates: Origin undocumented · credited to Franklin (1706–1790) without a source
answer.sourceLine: There is no Franklin source. His papers are digitised and full-text searchable at Founders Online, and neither the sentence nor the phrase ‘every two hundred years’ appears anywhere in them — or, for that matter, anywhere in the papers of the other six founders on the site. The popular long form (‘…because all governments become stale and corrupt after 200 years’) circulates only on quotation sites, none of which cite a document the search, returning nothing ↗.

source.excerpt: God forbid we should ever be 20. years without such a rebellion. ... The tree of liberty must be refreshed from time to time with the blood of patriots and tyrants. It is it's natural manure.
trail: Franklin’s writings are one of the best-indexed bodies of text in American history. Founders Online carries the Yale edition of his papers in full, searchable to the word — which means absence really is evidence. A phrase search for ‘every two hundred years’ across all seven founders’ papers returns zero results, and ‘revolution every’ returns eleven hits, none of them Franklin’s and none of them this run the search ↗.

The quotation-site versions have no citation of any kind — no letter, no pamphlet, no reported remark. Even some aggregators list the long form under ‘Unknown’ rather than Franklin. A Quora asker had already flagged it as apocryphal before we looked the question ↗.

The idea it echoes is real, but it belongs to Thomas Jefferson, and his number was twenty. Writing to William Stephens Smith from Paris on 13 November 1787 about Shays’ Rebellion, he said ‘God forbid we should ever be 20. years without such a rebellion’ — and, a few lines later, produced the tree-of-liberty sentence Jefferson’s letter ↗.
source.excerptNote: Not the quote on this page. This is Jefferson, writing to William Stephens Smith about Shays’ Rebellion — a different man, a different decade, and an interval of twenty years rather than two hundred. It is the closest genuine thing in the founders’ papers, which is probably how Franklin ended up wearing it.

author.name: Benjamin Franklin
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Franklin
author.bio: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) is the founder people reach for when they want a saying to sound both wise and faintly mischievous — he wrote aphorisms for a living in Poor Richard’s Almanack, so almost anything epigrammatic can be made to fit him. He also supplies the famous exit line about a republic ‘if you can keep it,’ which primes people to expect warnings about political decay from him. What he did not do was set a maintenance schedule for revolutions.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a clean case: a searchable author, a phrase that is not there, and a real quotation nearby that explains the confusion.

items.why: Franklin’s collected papers are online and searchable word by word. Neither ‘every two hundred years’ nor any sentence of this shape appears. With a corpus this well indexed, silence is close to proof the null result ↗.

The version quotation sites carry — ‘…because all governments become stale and corrupt after 200 years’ — is offered with no letter, date or publication behind it. Some aggregators file it under ‘Unknown,’ which is the honest answer.

items.who: Thomas Jefferson — different quote, different number
items.why: Jefferson wrote in 1787 that he hoped America would never go twenty years without a rebellion, and that the tree of liberty needs refreshing with the blood of patriots and tyrants. Twenty, not two hundred; Jefferson, not Franklin; and about a specific tax revolt in Massachusetts the letter ↗.

Jefferson also argued that each generation — which he reckoned at about nineteen years — should be free to remake its own laws and constitution. That is where the ‘refresh the system periodically’ instinct genuinely comes from, and it is again not a two-century clock and not Franklin.

misattribution.truthLine: No documented author. Franklin’s papers do not contain it; the nearest genuine sentiment is Jefferson’s in 1787, and his interval was twenty years Jefferson, 1787 ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Two hundred years is a suspiciously convenient number for an American audience: it puts the next scheduled revolution somewhere in living memory of the reader, which is precisely what makes the line quotable in an argument.

It also flatters Franklin’s reputation as the founder who saw the machinery ageing — the man who supposedly answered ‘a republic, if you can keep it.’ Attaching a decay clock to him feels right, which is exactly the reflex this site exists to interrupt.
context.detailsSummary: What Jefferson actually said, and when
detailsBody: 13 November 1787, Paris: writing to William Stephens Smith about Shays’ Rebellion, Jefferson calculates that thirteen states in eleven years have produced one rebellion — ‘one rebellion in a century and a half for each state.’
In the same paragraph: ‘God forbid we should ever be 20. years without such a rebellion.’
And then the famous image: the tree of liberty must be refreshed from time to time with the blood of patriots and tyrants.
That is a private letter about one tax revolt, written by a man in Paris who had not seen it — not a constitutional maintenance schedule.
Franklin, in the same years, was in Philadelphia helping write the constitution Jefferson was grumbling about.
context.pull: Jefferson said twenty years, about one rebellion, in a private letter. Somebody moved the decimal point and changed the name.
